subject: physics
title: Dangers of electromagnetic radiation
key_idea: The danger of an electromagnetic wave increases with its frequency. Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can damage body tissue, and the risk depends on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.

blocks.text: This section covers why some electromagnetic waves are more dangerous than others.

items.meaning: Radiation that can damage cells and cause the mutation of genes. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising.
A change in a gene (in DNA) that can lead to cancer.

items: The danger of an electromagnetic wave increases with its frequency.
Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have the highest frequencies, so they are hazardous to human body tissue.
Radio waves are not ionising, so they are not harmful in the same way.
The Earth's atmosphere absorbs gamma rays (and some ultraviolet) from the Sun, so less reaches people.

blocks.text: Waves are generated or absorbed by changes in atoms and in the nuclei of atoms, over a wide range of frequencies.

items: Gamma rays come from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
X-rays can be emitted when electrons in an atom change energy level.
The higher the frequency, the greater the danger.
Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are hazardous to body tissue.
Gamma rays originate from the nucleus of an atom.

results: Lower frequency, so less dangerous than ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

options.label: Infrared
results: Lower frequency, so less dangerous than ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

options.label: Ultraviolet
results: Damage to surface cells and eyes. Skin ageing and skin cancer. Eye conditions.
Hazardous. Higher frequency than visible light.

options.label: X-rays
results: Mutation of genes and damage to cells. Increased risk of cancer.
Ionising and very hazardous. Higher frequency than ultraviolet.

options.label: Gamma rays
results: Mutation of genes and damage to cells. Increased risk of cancer.
Ionising and very hazardous. The highest frequency in the spectrum.

items: Ultraviolet can make skin age early and increases the risk of skin cancer.
Ultraviolet can also damage the eyes.
X-rays and gamma rays can cause mutation of genes and cancer.
Microwaves heat cells inside the body and infrared causes skin burns.
Ultraviolet causes skin damage, premature ageing, skin cancer and eye damage.
X-rays and gamma rays cause mutations and cancer.

blocks.text: This section covers radiation dose and how the risk is kept low.

items.meaning: A measure of the risk of harm from exposing the body to radiation. It is measured in sieverts (Sv).
One thousandth of a sievert. 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.

items: The effect of radiation depends on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.
A larger dose means a greater risk of harm, such as cancer.
Taking many X-rays gives a large total dose, so a radiographer stands behind a screen that absorbs some of the X-rays.
Gamma rays from an injected isotope can irradiate the whole body for longer than an X-ray, which only exposes part of the body briefly.

blocks.label: Changing millisieverts to sieverts
blocks.formula: dose in sieverts = dose in millisieverts ÷ 1000
where: dose in sieverts is in sieverts (Sv).
dose in millisieverts is in millisieverts (mSv).

items: Radiation dose measures the risk of harm. The unit is the sievert (Sv).
1000 mSv = 1 Sv.
A larger dose carries a greater risk, so exposure is kept as low as possible.

checks.q: State two risks of exposure to high levels of ultraviolet radiation.
checks.a: Any two from: ageing of the skin, skin cancer, eye damage.

checks.q: Explain why gamma rays can be harmful but radio waves are not.
checks.a: Gamma rays are ionising but radio waves are not. Gamma rays can cause mutations in genes (DNA) or increase the risk of cancer.

worked_example.question:
To use X-rays for medical imaging, a machine produces a very brief burst of X-rays.

To use gamma rays for medical imaging, a radioactive isotope is injected into the patient's blood. The isotope is circulated around the body in the blood. The isotope emits gamma rays.

Compare the potential risks to a patient of using X-rays and gamma rays for medical imaging.
answer_points: Both are ionising radiation, so there is some risk of cancer.
The whole body is irradiated by gamma rays.
When an X-ray is taken, only part of the body is exposed.
The exposure time for gamma rays is longer.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each point. Make each point a comparison between the two methods.

worked_example.question:
Ultraviolet (UV) waves from the Sun travel towards the Earth.

Ultraviolet waves can be grouped by wavelength. The groups are UVA, UVB and UVC.

UVA: wavelength range 400 nm to 315 nm; 5% of energy absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere.
UVB: wavelength range 314 nm to 280 nm; 95% of energy absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere.
UVC: wavelength range 279 nm to 100 nm; 100% of energy absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere.

Explain why UVC is potentially the most dangerous ultraviolet radiation but does not cause harm to people.
answer_points: UVC has the smallest wavelength (highest frequency, highest energy, most ionising), so it is potentially the most dangerous.
It does not harm people because 100% of it is absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere, so none reaches the surface.
worked_example.tip: The answer needs a link: why it is dangerous, then why it does no harm.

worked_example.question:
Which type of wave is the most dangerous: infra-red, microwaves or X-rays?

Identify two reasons for your answer.
answer_points: Any two from: X-rays have the highest frequency, highest energy and shortest wavelength; they are ionising; they can cause cancer, damage cells or kill cells.
worked_example.tip: The two marks are still given if the wave chosen is wrong, but you should name X-rays.
